title: feat: add internal launch_server() to be compatible with _server.yml standard
description:
This PR adds and internal `launch_server()` function that makes `nanoext` compatible with the [`_server.yaml`](https://posit-dev.github.io/plumber2/articles/server_yml.html) standard introduced by plumber2. 

Notably, the `_server.yml` is quite minimal and only `engine` and `constructor` are required.

```yaml
engine: nanonext
constructor: server.R
options:
  host: 127.0.0.1
  port: 8080
```

Per the standard, `engine` must be equal to the package name `nanonext`.
Then, the `constructor` is a path to an R script that creates a handler or a list of handlers that are passed to `http_server()`.

`options` captures host and port and `tls`.

To be able to read the `_server.yml`, `yaml` is added as a suggested dependency.

title: Fix `ncurl()` double free on failed redirect follow-up (#351)
description:
Fixes #351.

`rnng_ncurl()` freed the transaction aio after a successful request without resetting the pointer. When a followed redirect then failed in `nng_http_client_alloc()` before re-allocation, the cleanup path freed the dangling pointer again, aborting the R process.

Surfaced on CRAN's Fedora checks: the system libnng 1.12.2 there lacks a working TLS engine, so the 301 to an HTTPS URL fails with `NNG_ENOTSUP` and hits this path. The bug itself is long-standing and platform-independent.

Fix: reset `aio` to `NULL` after freeing, consistent with the existing null-after-free handling of `res`/`req`/`client`/`cfg` in the redirect path.

title: Fix memory leaks in HTTP server teardown
description:
Fixes #339.

Fixes two ownership bugs in `http_server()`:

1. Handlers were never freed. `http_server_cleanup()` (and the creation failure path) removes each handler from the NNG server with `nng_http_server_del_handler()`, which is a pure list removal that returns ownership to the caller — the matching `nng_http_handler_free()` was missing, so every handler leaked once teardown ran. The removal itself remains necessary, as the handler's data pointer aims into the `srv->handlers` array about to be freed, and the underlying NNG server is port-cached and may outlive the R object. Freeing is safe against in-flight requests since NNG refcounts handlers during dispatch.
2. Streaming requests were never freed. Streaming handlers hijack the connection via `nng_http_hijack()`, which detaches both the connection and the request from NNG's ownership. The request pointer stored in the stream connection was never released. `nng_http_req_free()` is now called wherever the stream connection is destroyed — `conn_cleanup()`, the server cleanup fallback loop, and the two allocation-failure branches after hijacking.

The tests now also process the event loop once after the last HTTP server closes, so its deferred cleanup runs within the test process rather than being abandoned at exit.

title: Fix msg send memory leak
description:
Fixes #337.

`src/nng/src/core/msgqueue.c`
- `nni_msgq_aio_put()` now frees and clears the attached message when `nni_aio_begin()` fails.
- This closes the race where a pipe's `aio_put` is closed by `pipe_close` while the pipe's recv callback is still in flight with a freshly received message: `nni_aio_begin` returns `NNG_ECANCELED` without ever scheduling the completion, so the callback that would free the message never fires and `nni_aio_fini` doesn't free attached messages.
- The two added lines mirror the existing convention in the tcp and inproc transport send functions.

title: Fix use-after-free in bundled NNG TLS stream cancellation
description:
Closes #334.

Fixes the use-after-free detected by CRAN's valgrind checks on an ncurl() HTTPS timeout.

When a canceled aio is at the head of the TLS send/recv queue, upstream `tls_cancel` only aborts the underlying TCP aio — a no-op while it is idle (e.g. mid-handshake) — leaving the aio queued with iovs into buffers the HTTP layer has already released to the caller. When the handshake later completes, the freed request buffer is handed to the TLS engine.

This PR's patch (replayed via `tools/patch_nng.sh`) makes `tls_cancel` always dequeue and finish the canceled aio, keeping the abort so an in-flight TCP operation still unwinds.

title: Dispatcher: run the event handlers in the callbacks
description:
Removes the dispatcher loop thread. Previously, I/O completions signalled a condition variable shared with mirai's synchronization machinery and woke a dedicated thread, which processed the events and performed synchronous sends — a thread handoff per event, with sends serializing the pipeline. Event handling now runs directly in the I/O completion callbacks, serialized by a single private mutex, eliminating the handoff entirely.

Moving the work into the callbacks imposes three constraints that shape the design:

- **Callbacks must never block.** They run on a shared, finite thread pool, so a blocking send could starve the very threads needed to complete it. Every send is therefore asynchronous, with completions harvested lazily at the next event that implies they have finished.

- **The hot path cannot allocate or fail.** In callback context there is no one to report failure to. The task queue is intrusive — each node lives in the queued message's own header, making enqueue a plain memcpy — and all send/receive machinery is pooled and preallocated. Allocation survives only on cold paths with a sane fallback.

- **Lifecycle without an owning thread.** With no thread to join, correctness at disconnect and shutdown rests on event-ordering guarantees and lazy reaping of resources once their in-flight operations settle, rather than on a loop that owns everything.

Key efficiency savings per task cycle:

- **Two thread handoffs eliminated** — the host receive and the daemon reply were each signalled to the loop thread (cv wake plus context switch); both are now handled where they complete, and the loop thread itself is gone.
- **Sends no longer serialize the pipeline** — the loop performed sends synchronously, blocking all dispatch behind each one; sends are now asynchronous and, being callback-less, complete inline without scheduling any work onto the thread pool.
- **Zero heap allocation in steady state** — the per-task queue node malloc is gone (the node lives in the message's own header), and reply and receive machinery is drawn from preallocated pools.
- **Concurrent intake** — a pool of receive operations processes replies from multiple daemons in parallel, where the single loop handled one at a time; each reply's state update and forward now also happen under a single lock hold.

The dispatcher owns a private mutex/cv, decoupling it from mirai's shared cv; the C interface no longer takes the `cvar` argument, which survives R-side with a `NULL` default so mirai can drop it at leisure. External semantics are unchanged: FIFO ordering, serial/sync handling, RNG stream advancement, backpressure, and cancellation.

title: More efficient `race_aio()`
description:
Reworks `race_aio()` to use each aio's completion `result` as the resolution marker — the same one `aio_get_msg()` relies on — rather than polling `nng_aio_busy()` behind repeated environment lookups. This is both cheaper per scan and correctly synchronized with the cv signal, closing windows where a resolution racing with entry to the function could be missed or detected up to 400ms late.

The wait is now also a read-only observer of the condition variable, where previously it reset the cv on entry and consumed signals on wakeup. Those writes could steal a wakeup posted for another waiter on the same cv — with dispatcher, whose event loop waits on this very cv, a stolen signal could leave a task undelivered and hang a subsequent collect. This was the cause of a rare hang observed in the mirai test suite.

title: Add asynchronous streaming HTTP client
description:
## Summary

This adds a low-level asynchronous HTTP(S) response-body stream alongside `ncurl_aio()`.

`ncurl_aio()` remains the right interface when a caller wants one completed HTTP transaction. The new interface covers the different case where the response head must become available before the body is complete and body bytes must be consumed incrementally:

- `ncurl_stream_aio()` returns an `ncurlStreamAio` whose value contains   `status`, `headers`, and an `ncurlStream`;
- `ncurl_stream_recv()` returns a `recvAio` resolving to raw `data` and   a `complete` flag, with optional condition-variable signalling;
- `close()` explicitly releases the stream and cancels an active   receive;
- `is_ncurl_stream()` identifies the connection handle.

The opening and receive operations use nanonext’s existing Aio, active-binding, `later`, promises, and `errorValue` conventions.

## Motivation

The immediate downstream use is [Rho](https://github.com/sounkou-bioinfo/Rho), an asynchronous provider and agent runtime for R. OpenAI, Anthropic, GitHub Copilot, and other model APIs return Server-Sent Events over HTTP. Waiting for the complete response body would prevent Rho from emitting text deltas, reasoning updates, and tool calls while the request is active. It would also delay useful cancellation until the provider finishes the response.

Rho keeps the layers separate:

``` text
nanonext HTTP response head and body Aios
  -> rho.http raw body stream
  -> rho.http SSE events
  -> rho.ai typed provider events
  -> rho.agent lifecycle events
```

The SSE and provider protocols do not belong in nanonext. Conversely, opening a raw TCP/TLS stream and implementing HTTP response framing in R would duplicate transport behavior already owned by nanonext and NNG. This change supplies the small transport primitive between those two layers.

The same primitive is also applicable to NDJSON, progressive downloads, and other long-lived HTTP response bodies.

## Executable example

This example uses nanonext’s local HTTP server. The client receives the first event, the still-open server connection sends a second event, and only then is the response completed.

``` r
library(nanonext)

stream_example <- function() {
  server_connection <- NULL
  client_stream <- NULL

  server <- http_server(
    url = "http://127.0.0.1:0",
    handlers = list(handler_stream(
      "/events",
      on_request = function(connection, request) {
        server_connection <<- connection
        connection$set_status(200L)
        connection$set_header("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
        connection$send(format_sse(data = "first"))
      }
    ))
  )
  stopifnot(server$start() == 0L)
  on.exit({
    if (!is.null(client_stream)) try(close(client_stream), silent = TRUE)
    if (!is.null(server_connection)) try(server_connection$close(), silent = TRUE)
    try(server$close(), silent = TRUE)
  }, add = TRUE)

  collect_event <- function(stream) {
    bytes <- raw()
    repeat {
      receive_cv <- cv()
      receiving <- ncurl_stream_recv(
        stream,
        timeout = 2000L,
        cv = receive_cv
      )
      stopifnot(until(receive_cv, 2000L))
      chunk <- receiving$data
      stopifnot(!is_error_value(chunk))
      bytes <- c(bytes, chunk$data)
      if (endsWith(rawToChar(bytes), "\n\n") || chunk$complete) {
        return(list(data = bytes, complete = chunk$complete))
      }
    }
  }

  opening <- ncurl_stream_aio(
    paste0(server$url, "/events"),
    headers = c(Accept = "text/event-stream"),
    timeout = 2000L,
    buffer = 1L
  )
  while (unresolved(opening)) later::run_now(0.01)
  response <- opening$data
  stopifnot(!is_error_value(response), response$status == 200L)
  client_stream <- response$stream

  first <- collect_event(client_stream)
  stopifnot(
    server_connection$send(format_sse(data = "second")) == 0L
  )
  second <- collect_event(client_stream)
  stopifnot(server_connection$close() == 0L)

  ending <- ncurl_stream_recv(client_stream, timeout = 2000L)
  while (unresolved(ending)) later::run_now(0.01)
  end <- ending$data
  stopifnot(!is_error_value(end), end$complete)

  event_data <- function(value) {
    line <- strsplit(rawToChar(value$data), "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1L]][1L]
    sub("^data: ", "", line)
  }

  data.frame(
    receive = c("first", "second", "end"),
    data = c(event_data(first), event_data(second), rawToChar(end$data)),
    complete = c(first$complete, second$complete, end$complete)
  )
}

stream_example()
#>   receive   data complete
#> 1   first  first    FALSE
#> 2  second second    FALSE
#> 3     end            TRUE
```

Chunks are raw entity-body bytes. Message framing above the HTTP body, such as SSE line assembly, remains the caller’s responsibility.

## Implementation

The C implementation uses NNG’s HTTP client connection API in three opening phases: connect, write the request, and read the response head. It then performs one asynchronous body read at a time.

HTTP/1.1 response bodies are framed as follows:

- `HEAD`, informational, `204`, and `304` responses complete without a   body;
- `Content-Length` responses complete after the declared number of   bytes;
- chunked transfer coding is decoded before bytes are returned to R;
- otherwise, connection close terminates the body.

The stream owns its URL, client, request, response, TLS hold, connection, and mutex. External-pointer finalizers release those resources. The stream external pointer is protected by each active Aio, only one receive may be active, and closing the stream closes the NNG connection so a pending receive resolves with an `errorValue`.

A receive timeout is terminal. Continuing after an interrupted partial NNG read would leave the framing state ambiguous, so later receives return the stored error.

## Cancellation and completion delivery

The new opening and receive types enter the existing Aio collection, wait-thread, and promise-context switches. `stop_aio()` resolves a cancelled receive to an `errorValue`; that cancellation is terminal because the read may have advanced the HTTP framing state. `close()` marks the owning stream closed and closes the HTTP connection, completing an active receive with an `errorValue`. Active Aios protect the stream external pointer until their callbacks and finalizers have finished.

## API consistency

Both opening and body receive objects inherit from `recvAio`, so `unresolved()`, `call_aio()`, `collect_aio()`, `stop_aio()`, and
promises retain their existing behavior. A body receive also accepts `cv`, including for immediately resolved completion and error values. Failed opens retain the `ncurlStreamAio` subclass, and closed or failed streams return resolved `errorValue` receives. Invalid objects and overlapping receives remain usage errors. The `ncurlStream` print state distinguishes open, complete, error, and closed lifecycles.

The comparison is split into three commits: the C/Aio transport, the public R surface with roxygen-generated documentation, and the framing/lifecycle tests.

## Deliberate initial scope

- The stream sends `Connection: close`; connection pooling and reuse are
  not part of this API.
- Redirects are returned to the caller rather than followed.
- Content encodings are not decompressed.
- Chunked response trailers are consumed but not exposed.
- The client returns bytes and does not interpret SSE or another
  application protocol.

## Validation

The added nanonext tests exercise:

- response-head resolution before the response body is complete;
- incremental SSE delivery with a one-byte receive buffer, splitting
  framing across arbitrary read boundaries;
- clean end-of-stream and repeated reads after completion;
- condition-variable signalling for pending and immediately resolved
  receives;
- rejection of concurrent receives;
- cancellation while the response head is pending;
- closing while a receive is active;
- direct `stop_aio()` cancellation and the resulting terminal stream
  error;
- terminal receive timeout behavior;
- HTTPS streaming with a supplied in-memory TLS configuration.

The downstream `rho.http` test consumes one SSE event while the server
connection remains open, sends a second event, and observes a typed end
after the server closes.

Local validation:

``` text
NOT_CRAN=true R CMD check --no-manual
Status: OK

R 4.6.0, Ubuntu 24.04

rho.http package tests against the checked nanonext build
34 results, all OK (15 incremental streaming assertions)

git diff --check
clean
```

The draft is intended to get early review of the public API, body-framing state machine, and connection/Aio ownership before the interface is treated as settled.

## LLM usage

Codex with `gpt-5.6-sol` at maximum reasoning effort was used to help write the code, tests, PR draft, and documentation. I tested the changes and take responsibility for this contribution.

title: Silent error handling for server callbacks
description:
- When an HTTP server request handler signals an error, the server maps it to a `500 Internal Server Error` response; previously the R error condition was also printed to the console, producing stray `Error:` output even though the error was fully handled.
- The handler is invoked in `http_invoke_callback()` (`src/server.c`) via `R_tryEval`, which catches the error (returned through the `err` flag) *and* prints it to stderr; since the caller already inspects `err` and returns a 500, that print is redundant.
- Switches to `R_tryEvalSilent`, keeping the identical catch-and-map-to-500 behaviour while suppressing the console output.

title: Add `device_aio()` to relay messages between two Sockets
description:
Exposes NNG's device facility — a zero-copy forwarder that relays raw messages between two Sockets — as `device_aio()`. This is the building block for brokers and proxies, such as a pub/sub relay or a pair-to-pair bridge.

Only the asynchronous `nng_device_aio()` form is wrapped; the blocking `nng_device()` would freeze the R session. The device runs on NNG's background threads until it is stopped (`stop_aio()`) or a Socket closes, mirroring the `send_aio()` / `recv_aio()` naming.

### How it works

`device_aio(s1, s2 = s1)` returns a `sendAio`. Both Sockets must be opened in raw mode and use complementary protocols (each's peer protocol must be the other's protocol, e.g. two `pair` Sockets, or a `pub` and a `sub`). Passing the same Socket for both arguments creates a reflector. The returned aio resolves only when the device stops: `$result` is an `unresolved` NA while running, and otherwise the integer exit code (typically the error that stopped it, such as a Socket being closed).

The implementation reuses the existing result-only aio machinery rather than adding a new type. A device produces an integer result and no message — exactly the `IOV_SENDAIO` shape — so it borrows that type's `(callback, finalizer)` pair (`isaio_complete` + `saio_finalizer` with `nano_list_do` deferred free), and both R-side dispatch switches (`rnng_aio_call`, `rnng_unresolved_impl`) already route `IOV_SENDAIO` to the result path unchanged. Both Socket objects are stored in the aio's external-pointer protected slot so a running device cannot be broken by premature GC of its Sockets.

title: Prune the unused NNG logging subsystem from the build

Accept a named list for the `ncurl()` headers argument
description:
`ncurl()`, `ncurl_aio()` and `ncurl_session()` now accept a named list for the `headers` argument, in addition to the existing named character vector. This restores behaviour that the package supported in early versions.

The 3 `ncurl*` C entry points each carried an identical inline block that only handled `STRSXP`. These are replaced by a single shared helper `nano_set_req_headers()` that switches on the SEXP type:

- `STRSXP` (named character vector) — each element is set as a header, as before.
- `VECSXP` (named list) — each element is taken via its first string element; non-character elements are skipped.

In both cases an argument without a valid names attribute is ignored.

The `headers` documentation is updated to describe both forms, and the `response` argument docs are tidied to lead with `TRUE` (return all headers) followed by the character-vector form.

title: Pre-release fixes and cleanups
description:
A set of small, self-contained fixes and cleanups ahead of the next release, one per commit.

- Fix recv(mode = "character") dropping elements: the decoder under-allocated string slots and truncated; it now counts segments exactly so a received character vector matches what was sent, preserving empty strings in all positions.
- Bind each ncurl_aio active binding once: added break to a fall-through switch that bound status/headers/data 6 times instead of 3.
- Scan for the string terminator with memchr in nano_raw_char, replacing a hand loop whose int counter gave a signed/unsigned comparison and UB for buffers larger than INT_MAX.
- Define the nano context_open closure once instead of duplicating it byte-for-byte across the req/rep, sub, surveyor, and respondent branches.
- Give file-local functions internal linkage: single_wait_thread_create, nano_readline, nano_read_thread, and delayed_sigterm are marked static.
- Correct the nng_structs.h version comment from >= 1.11.0 to >= 1.12.0 to match the current minimum supported libnng.

title: HTTP Rest Server
description:
_Experimental_

Permits evaluation of arbitrary R expressions submitted to an API endpoint.

Client-neutral, supporting any HTTP client.

Run server in a new session:
```
Rscript -e 'nanonext::server("http://127.0.0.1:5555/api/rest")'
```
Query using command line `curl`:
```
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5555/api/rest -d 'format(Sys.time())'
```

Query from within R:
```r
ncurl("http://127.0.0.1:5555/api/rest", method = "POST", data = "format(Sys.time())")

res <- ncurl(
  "http://127.0.0.1:5555/api/rest",
  convert = FALSE,
  method = "POST",
  data = "data.frame(random = nanonext::random(3))"
)
unserialize(res$data)

```
Result is returned as a string where possible supporting non-R clients e.g. command line `curl`.
Otherwise as a binary R-serialized object, which may be consumed by an R client.

title: R callbacks and promises
description:
This is a sketch of how we could safely and efficiently get R callbacks when aio operations complete.

```r
library(nanonext)
library(promises)

socket1 <- socket("req", listen = "inproc://nanonext")
socket2 <- socket("rep", dial = "inproc://nanonext")

recv_aio(socket2) %...>% message("Received message: ", .)

send(socket1, "hello world!")
```

should print "Received message: hello world!" at the console.

### Design

The C functions `rnng_recv_aio` and `rnng_recv_aio_signal` take an additional R function argument, which if non-NULL will be invoked on the main R thread at the top of the `later` event loop.

The R functions `recv_aio` and `recv_aio_signal` take advantage of this to support a `$callback` member on the recvAio environment; if present at the time the request is completed, it will be invoked with the value or error. (If `$callback` is set _after_ the request is completed, it will never be invoked.)

The `as.promise.recvAio` uses `$callback` to implement promise resolution.

### A note on API

For this proof of concept, I enhanced both `recv_aio` and `recv_aio_signal` to support `$callback` but have no idea if this is what you'd want to do. As written, every recv_aio operation will cause later to invoke an R callback, even if it's not used. I haven't measured the impact of this performance-wise, but given how lean nanonext runs, it seems like you might want this behavior to be opt-in. Like maybe `recv_aio` and `recv_aio_signal` can't be coerced to promises, but a new `recv_aio_async` returns a promise directly?

Also, I didn't implement this for the send functions but I imagine it would work in much the same way.

title: Trim unused mbedTLS modules from the bundle and build
description:
Disables four mbedTLS modules that nanonext never uses and drops their now-dead sources, trimming the bundle and build. Companion to the NNG prune in #303.

## What's removed

Four modules are disabled in `mbedtls_config.h` and their sources dropped:

- `MBEDTLS_HKDF_C` (`hkdf.c`) — HKDF is a TLS 1.3 / PSA key-schedule primitive; both are off (TLS 1.2 only), so it has no consumer.
- `MBEDTLS_SSL_CACHE_C` (`ssl_cache.c`) — server-side session cache; nng never wires it up.
- `MBEDTLS_SSL_TICKET_C` (`ssl_ticket.c`) — the built-in session-ticket implementation; nng never installs the ticket callbacks. The `MBEDTLS_SSL_SESSION_TICKETS` protocol extension is kept.
- `MBEDTLS_X509_CSR_WRITE_C` (`x509write_csr.c`) — CSR writing; nanonext generates self-signed CRTs (`x509write_crt`, kept), never CSRs.

Two further sources were already empty objects on every architecture and are dropped too: `block_cipher.c` (`MBEDTLS_BLOCK_CIPHER_C` off) and `ssl_debug_helpers_generated.c` (`MBEDTLS_DEBUG_C` off).

The orphaned `ssl_cache.h` / `ssl_ticket.h` headers are removed. `hkdf.h`, `block_cipher.h` and `ssl_debug_helpers.h` are retained because compiled units still include them (their contents are macro-guarded, so harmless).

## How it works

`tools/mbedtls.list` loses the six object lines and the three Makevars are regenerated from it via `tools/generate_makevars.sh`; `configure` reads the list directly. mbedTLS's `check_config.h` confirms nothing else requires the disabled modules.

The hardware-AES pair `aesni.c` (x86) and `aesce.c` (arm64) is retained — each is an empty object on the other architecture but live on its own, so both are needed for cross-platform builds.

`tools/update_mbedtls.sh` is intentionally left unchanged: it carries no prune step for the existing hand-trimmed upstream sources, so the mbedTLS list/config/tree remain hand-maintained as before.

title: Drop unused vendored NNG sources from the bundle and build
description:
Prunes three vendored NNG source units that nanonext never uses, trimming the bundle and build.

## What's removed

- `supplemental/websocket/stub.c` — the websocket *disabled* stub. Upstream compiles it only when websocket support is off; nanonext always builds the real `websocket.c` (which defines the same `nni_ws_*` symbols), so the stub is never compiled and would clash if it were.
- `supplemental/util/idhash.c` (+ header) — the public `nng_id_map` API. nanonext uses the internal `nni_id_map` from `core/idhash.c` (retained) instead.
- `supplemental/util/options.c` (+ header) — `nng_opts_parse`, a CLI argument parser for NNG's own demos/tools.

The two removed headers were each included only by their own `.c`, so nothing else in the tree references any of this.

## How it works

The removals are wired into the vendoring contract so a future re-vendor keeps dropping them:

- `idhash.c` / `options.c` *are* compiled by the cmake oracle, so they're added to `PRUNE_RE` in `tools/update_nng.sh` (which filters the derived object lists and keeps `--verify` consistent), and removed from `tools/nng_common.list`.
- `stub.c` is never in the oracle (we build with websocket on), so it's dropped via an explicit `rm` in the staging step rather than `PRUNE_RE`. The two orphaned headers are removed the same way (`PRUNE_RE` only covers objects).
- The three Makevars are regenerated from the lists via `tools/generate_makevars.sh`; `configure` reads the `.list` files directly, so no change there.

title: Re-vendor bundled NNG from upstream, and fix TLS config reuse
description:
## Summary

This branch does two things:

1. **Replaces the bundled copy of NNG with the real upstream source.** The old `src/nng` was a hand-edited snapshot that had drifted from upstream and was hard to audit. It's now the actual upstream NNG `stable` tree at a pinned commit (`45f8116f`), kept as *"upstream plus a short list of documented edits"* so anyone can regenerate and verify it.

2. **Fixes a "Resource busy" error when a TLS config is re-used.** Pulling in current NNG also pulled in a stricter rule (see below), which broke re-using one `tls_config()` object for more than one connection. The second commit restores that.

## How it works

**The re-vendor**

- The exact upstream commit is pinned in `tools/update_nng.sh`. Running that script re-fetches it, removes cmake, re-applies our edits, and regenerates the build file lists automatically.
- Our edits are deliberately minimal and documented (a version string, silencing NNG's debug/logging output so CRAN's compiled-code checks stay clean, and a few compiler-warning fixes). They're replayed by `tools/patch_nng.sh`.
- It's fully reproducible: after re-running the update script, `git diff src/nng` is empty, and `--verify` cross-checks the build lists against a fresh cmake reference.

**The TLS fix**

- Current NNG treats a TLS configuration as **read-only once it has been used for a connection**. nanonext sets the server name (SNI) on the config every time it dials, so the *second* use of a re-used config failed with `4 | Resource busy`.
- We can't just stop setting the server name: modern mbedTLS refuses an authenticated client handshake unless it's set, and we can't work around that inside NNG because nanonext may be built against a system `libnng` we don't control.
- So the fix simply **ignores the "busy" error when re-applying the server name to a config that's already in use** — the name is already set, so there's nothing more to do. Re-using a config now works again, across `comms.c` (dial), `ncurl.c`, and `proto.c` (streams). One caveat: a single config re-used against *different* hostnames stays pinned to the first one (later mismatched connections fail safely instead of connecting insecurely).

title: Reserve message headroom when installing a serialized buffer body
description:
## Summary

Fixes message-body corruption that surfaces when nanonext is linked against a separately-built `libnng` (e.g. the released 1.11.0 on R-universe's Linux images): serialized messages round-trip as unserializable garbage and `R CMD check` fails in the test phase.

## How it works

`nano_msg_set_body` installs the serialization buffer as a message body zero-copy by writing the body chunk fields directly, with `ch_ptr == ch_buf` — i.e. **zero headroom**. A native `nng_msg` always carries ~32 bytes of leading headroom (the `sz + 32, 32` in `nni_msg_alloc`) so protocols can prepend their header in place.

With zero headroom, the header prepend on the inproc req/rep path (`nni_msg_pull_up` → `nni_chunk_insert`) is forced down a branch whose implementation differs between NNG versions. The bundled NNG handles it correctly; a released 1.11.0 `nni_chunk_insert` (a rewritten "split/centre" variant) writes the header over the start of the body, mangling it — length preserved, content garbage, so the receiver reports "received data could not be unserialized". This is a source difference in `message.c`, not a build/config difference, and it is latent for the bundled build too (a future NNG re-vendor would hit it).

This reserves `NANO_HEADROOM` (32, matching NNG's native allocation) at the front during serialization and points the donated body past it: `ch_ptr = ch_buf + headroom`, `ch_len = cur - headroom`, `ch_cap = cur`. The donated message is then structurally identical to a native `nng_msg` (headroom 32, room 32), so the prepend stays on the in-place `len <= headroom` branch on every NNG version. The raw/encode and dispatcher buffers pass headroom 0 (behaviour unchanged).

title: Remove cmake from the build; compile bundled libraries in place
description:
Closes #299.

## Summary

Removes the build-time dependency on **cmake**. The bundled NNG and Mbed TLS sources are now compiled directly into `nanonext.so`/`.dll` via explicit per-object rules in the Makevars — no cmake, no static archives, no install step. Installation needs only a C compiler. A system `libnng` (>= 1.11) and `libmbedtls` (>= 2.5) continue to be used when present.

This follows the compile-in-place pattern used in `watcher`, scaled to two C libraries (NNG ~86 objects, Mbed TLS 64).

On a platform that cannot compile the bundled NNG at all, installation falls back to a non-functional stub rather than failing, so dependents stay installable everywhere.

## How it works

- **`configure`** detects system libs; otherwise ports NNG's POSIX feature probes (`check_function_exists`/`check_symbol_exists`/`check_library_exists`/`check_struct_has_member`) to portable `/bin/sh`, sets the `NNG_HAVE_*` macros, selects exactly one poller (`port_create`/`kqueue`/`epoll`+`eventfd`/`poll`) and one random source (`arc4random`/`getrandom`/`urandom`), then substitutes the flags + object lists into `src/Makevars.in`. Its `-D` output was validated byte-for-byte against a `compile_commands.json` cmake oracle.
- **`src/Makevars.in` / `.win` / `.ucrt`** are generated artifacts (explicit per-object rules, no GNU-make dependency). Windows is fully static (no `configure.win`/`.ucrt`); biarch is served by R's per-sub-arch build.
- **`tools/`** is the single source of truth: `*.list` object lists, `generate_makevars.sh`, and `update_{nng,mbedtls}.sh` (with `--verify` to diff the lists against a fresh cmake oracle — the drift guard). `patch_{nng,mbedtls}.sh` neuter the compiled-code diagnostics.
- `$(C_VISIBILITY)` (`-fvisibility=hidden`) reaches every bundled object, hiding the `nng_*`/`mbedtls_*` symbols (now 0 exported, was 427 + 754).
- All `CMakeLists.txt` and `cmake/` trees deleted from `src/nng` and `src/mbedtls`.

- **Unsupported-platform fallback**: when bundling, `configure` probes (compile-only) for the pthread/socket headers NNG's POSIX layer needs. On a genuinely non-POSIX target that lacks them it builds a stub instead of failing — `generate_stub` emits `src/stub.c` registering every routine from `init.c`'s `callMethods[]` bound to a single `Rf_error`, with a trivial `OBJECTS = stub.o` Makevars — so the package installs and loads (functions error when called).

title: Free NNG receive buffer eagerly after decode
description:
## Summary

- Free NNG receive buffer in `create_aio_msg()` immediately after `nano_decode()` copies data into the R object, rather than deferring to the external pointer finalizer

## Rationale

After `nano_decode()` copies received data into a new R SEXP, the source NNG buffer (either `malloc`'d for IOV receives or an `nng_msg` for message receives) is no longer needed. Previously it was freed only when R's garbage collector ran the aio's finalizer.

R's GC is pressure-driven but only tracks R heap allocations — it has no visibility into external `malloc`'d or NNG-allocated memory. Between GC cycles, stale NNG buffers from resolved aios accumulate as invisible external memory. Eager freeing makes cleanup deterministic and prevents this accumulation, particularly when resolving many aios in quick succession.

Setting `raio->data = NULL` after freeing is safe because both `iaio_finalizer` and `raio_finalizer` already guard with `if (xp->data != NULL)`.

title: Threaded in-process dispatcher
description:
### Summary

- Move the task dispatcher off R's main thread onto a dedicated C thread, allowing the host R process to remain responsive while the dispatcher manages daemon connections and task routing
- Add direct cancellation that operates on dispatcher state under mutex, replacing the previous round-trip of sending cancellation messages through NNG contexts
- Implement L'Ecuyer-CMRG RNG stream advancement in pure C, eliminating the R callback during daemon initialization

### Design

The dispatcher thread runs an event loop driven by NNG AIO callbacks that wake a shared condition variable. A `nano_dispatcher_handle` wraps the dispatcher, its sockets, monitor, and thread — exposed to R as an external pointer with a C finalizer for cleanup. The shared CV lets the host R process coordinate with the dispatcher thread for waiting on connections, reading stats, and throttling via a limit gate.

### Other changes

- `nano_saio.ctx` replaced by `nano_saio.disp` pointer enabling direct cancellation from `request_complete` and `rnng_request_stop`

title: HTTP Streaming Support (including SSE)
description:
Extension to the HTTP Server #240.
                                       
This PR adds `handler_stream()` for HTTP streaming using chunked transfer encoding, building on the existing HTTP server infrastructure. Supports any streaming HTTP protocol including Server-Sent Events (SSE), newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON), and custom streaming formats.

## New Features

`handler_stream(path, on_request, on_close, method, prefix)`
  - Creates HTTP streaming endpoints using chunked transfer encoding
  - Hijacks the HTTP connection for long-lived server-to-client streaming

`format_sse(data, event, id, retry)`
  - Helper to format messages per SSE specification
  - Handles multi-line data, event types, IDs, and retry intervals

 Connection object methods:
  - `conn$send(data)` - Send chunk to this connection
  - `conn$close()` - Close connection (sends terminal chunk)
  - `conn$set_status(code)` - Set HTTP status (before first send)
  - `conn$set_header(name, value)` - Set response header (before first send)
  - `conn$id` - Unique connection identifier

## Architecture

Refactored connection handling to use a base `nano_conn` struct that both WebSocket (`nano_ws_conn`) and HTTP streaming (`nano_stream_conn`) connections inherit from. This enables code reuse for:
  - Connection lifecycle management
  - Linked list tracking per handler
  - Unique server-wide connection IDs

## Example Usage

```r
# NDJSON streaming endpoint
handler_stream("/stream", function(conn, req) {
  conn$set_header("Content-Type", "application/x-ndjson")
  conn$send('{"status":"connected"}\n')
})

# SSE endpoint
handler_stream("/events", function(conn, req) {
  conn$set_header("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
  conn$set_header("Cache-Control", "no-cache")
  conn$send(format_sse(data = "connected"))
})

#  Long-lived streaming with broadcast:
conns <- list()
handlers <- list(
  handler_stream("/stream",
    on_request = function(conn, req) {
      conn$set_header("Content-Type", "application/x-ndjson")
      conns[[as.character(conn$id)]] <<- conn
      conn$send('{"status":"connected"}\n')
    },
    on_close = function(conn) {
      conns[[as.character(conn$id)]] <<- NULL
    }
  ),
  # POST endpoint triggers broadcast to all streaming clients
  handler("/broadcast", function(req) {
    msg <- paste0('{"msg":"', rawToChar(req$body), '"}\n')
    lapply(conns, function(c) c$send(msg))
    list(status = 200L, body = "sent")
  }, method = "POST")
)
```

Adds HTTP and WebSocket server support. New `http_server()` and `handler()` functions let nanonext serve HTTP requests and handle bidirectional WebSocket connections (HTTP/HTTPS/WS/WSS).                                                                     

Key Features:
- Dynamic handlers: `handler()` for custom R functions that process requests and return responses                                                                                
- WebSocket handlers: `handler_ws()` with `on_open`, `on_message`, and `on_close` callbacks, plus unique connection IDs (`ws$id`) for tracking clients across all handlers

HTTP handlers and WebSocket listeners share NNG's underlying HTTP server on the same port
- the WS listener handles the RFC 6455 upgrade handshake automatically.                 
                                                                                           
WebSocket callbacks (`on_open`, `on_message`, `on_close`) run on R's main thread via later. Connection state is mutex-protected to avoid races between NNG's threads and R.          
                                                                                           
Other changes:

This PR allocates a `nng_msg` upfront and uses `nng_msg_append()` directly in all the internal encoding and serialization functions to avoid allocation of an intermediate object and memcpy - reducing peak memory usage.

title: NNG Protocol Level Memory Enhancements
description:
The mirai v2.0 architectural enhancement already improves memory usage, as we moved from:
```
host <-- `req/rep`--> dispatcher <-- `req/rep` --> daemon
```
to:
```
host <-- `req/rep`--> dispatcher <-- `poly` --> daemon
```
The `poly` protocol does not retain messages longer than necessary and is efficient in that regard.

This PR adds memory optimization for the remaining `req/rep` leg:

- The requestor on host still retains a copy of the message until the reply is received. This is even the case when we've turned off NNG's automatic protocol-level retry mechanism.
- The NNG source is patched to free the request message early as soon as the initial send is complete (as it won't be used again).
- Substantially lower memory usage on host if many mirai requests are outstanding (for example in a map operation).

The NNG author has previously agreed that this would be a sensible amendment to the protocol, so if everything tests out here, the patch will be proposed to upstream.

title: Makes Serial Config an Open Standard
description:
Previously `serial_config()` performed validation and created a specially-formatted object (constructable only through the R C API). The advantage of this was this didn't need to be re-validated at the point of being set.

However this prevents a 3rd party being able to simply create a configuration as a list without using the special constructor. This is somewhat inconsistent with what `mirai` (which this function supports) uses as a design concept elsewhere e.g. SSH configs created by `mirai::ssh_config()` are just simple lists).

Now validation occurs upon option setting as well, which is more robust behaviour as well as addressing the above.

This was only required to keep a reference to the associated tls configuration where present. We can tie the object lifetimes together using the PTR_PROT field of the SEXP instead.

This is more efficient for inproc/ipc/tcp everywhere where TLS is not relevant. Even for TLS, this provides for a cleaner and simpler approach.

- Uses stack-allocated objects where possible for memory safety
- Much more efficient with re-use of Aios etc.

This is a straight port of existing dispatcher using `inproc` sockets, only somewhat optimised. To keep things as light as possible, there is currently limited information retrieval from the dispatcher thread.
